kuai-mao.title: "Kuài" or "máo"?
kuai-mao.body: In spoken Chinese money, kuài (块) is the main unit (like "a dollar"), and máo (毛) is a tenth of a kuài (like "ten cents"). The structure simply puts the two numbers one after the other.

kuai-mao-yuan-jiao.title: "Kuài"/"máo" are what you SAY — "yuán"/"jiǎo" is what you WRITE
kuai-mao-yuan-jiao.body: Kuài and máo are the forms you will HEAR all the time in daily life. But on printed prices, receipts and in the news, you often see the formal/written forms: yuán (元, equivalent to kuài) and jiǎo (角, equivalent to máo). Nobody says "yuán" in casual conversation, but it is worth recognizing in writing.
examples: yuán = unit of money (written/formal form of 块)
jiǎo = a tenth of a yuán (written/formal form of 毛)

ba-particle.title: 吧 (ba) — softening a request or suggestion
ba-particle.body: 吧 (ba) at the end of a sentence turns a direct command into something softer, like a suggestion or polite request — similar to adding "okay?" or "come on" at the end of a sentence in English.
examples: make it a bit cheaper, come on

classifiers-more.title: More measure words
classifiers-more.body: You have already seen that every number needs a measure word before the noun (个/口, back in Unit 4). Just as 口 is specific to counting family members, other categories of things have their own measure word — like 件 for clothes.

pechinchar-mercado.title: Haggling is normal — but only in certain places
pechinchar-mercado.body: Notice how the price dropped from 30 to 25 kuài in the dialogue: in street markets, fairs and small neighborhood shops, haggling over the price is normal and even expected. But in malls, supermarkets and brand-name stores, prices are fixed and haggling feels out of place — the key is to recognize the type of place before trying.
examples: make it a bit cheaper (a typical phrase when haggling)
